claim: The proportion of good-faith Wikipedia newcomers who 'survive' (make at least one edit 2-6 months after their first edit session) declined from 35.7% for the first-half-2004 cohort to 11.3% for the second-half-2010 cohort.
stance_target: Wikipedia has a documented, quantified person-level cohort-survival curve for editors, operationalized as a 2-6-month post-first-session retention rate
scope_conditions: English Wikipedia only; newcomers sampled 2001-2011; not necessarily generalizable to other-language wikis
quoted_support: we observe a steady decline in the survival of "good-faith" from 35.7% in the first semester of 2004 to 11.3% in the second semester of 2010.

claim: Retention of the highest-quality ('golden') Wikipedia newcomers collapsed sharply from 40.0% to 13.2% specifically between the second half of 2006 and the first half of 2007, coinciding with the onset of Wikipedia's overall editor decline.
stance_target: The decline in Wikipedia active-editor counts is driven by a sudden retention collapse rather than gradual quality decay
quoted_support: "Golden" editors saw the most dramatic decrease in retention between the last semester of 2006 and the first semester of 2007 where the rate of survival went from 40.0% to 13.2% of newcomers.

claim: The sample underlying Wikipedia's newcomer quality/survival study consisted of 100 randomly sampled newcomers per 6-month period from 2001 to 2011, each rated by 5 coders on their first 'edit session' (avg. 3.67 edits, defined as edits within 1 hour of each other) into 4 quality classes.
stance_target: methodology and sample size of the Wikipedia editor cohort-survival study
quoted_support: Users from Wikipedia were randomly sampled such that each 6 month period between 2001 and 2011 contained 100 newcomers who performed their first article edit during that 6 month period.

claim: The rate at which good-faith Wikipedia newcomers had at least one first-session edit rejected (reverted or deleted) jumped from 15.7% to 48.6% between 2005 and 2006.
stance_target: rising quality-control rejection, not declining newcomer quality, is the proximate cause of falling newcomer retention
quoted_support: The Newcomer rejection over time plot shows that good-faith editors experienced a significant jump in the rate of rejection (15.7% to 48.6%) between 2005 and 2006

claim: The proportion of newcomers who are 'good-faith' or 'golden' quality (i.e., trying or succeeding at productive editing) has remained relatively flat since 2006, averaging 38.4% (good-faith) and 36.3% (golden) of newcomers, ruling out declining newcomer quality as the cause of the retention decline.
stance_target: the hypothesis that Wikipedia's editor decline is explained by an influx of lower-quality newcomers
quoted_support: Good-faith and golden newcomers represent 38.4% and 36.3% on average from 2006 forward respectively. This result suggests that any increase in rejection or decline in participation from the middle of the exponential growth period forward could not be attributed to a decrease in the quality of new editors.

claim: Between the first semester of 2005 and the first semester of 2006, the proportion of 'golden' (immediately productive) newcomers fell from 61.2% to 40.9%, with a partially offsetting rise in 'good-faith' (trying but not yet successful) newcomers from 24.3% to 42.0%.
stance_target: composition shift in newcomer quality classes during Wikipedia's exponential growth period
quoted_support: Between the first semester of 2005 and the first semester of 2006, we observe a substantial decline (61.2% to 40.9%) in the number of golden contributors, but also a smaller increase in the amount of good-faith contributors (24.3% to 42.0%).
